title: 5 changes that could help immigrant children detained in Connecticut - CT Insider
authors: Jacqueline Rabe Thomas, Joshua Eaton, Staff Writers
description:
Add Preferred Source Connecticut can't force the federal government to release detained immigrant children faster, although its Democratic leaders would want to.
Advertisement Article continues below this ad Here are five changes advocates say could alter the system.
Under the administration of President Joe Biden, the federal government released more than 1,000 immigrant children a year to sponsors living in Connecticut, federal data shows.
The six children whose lawyers filed lawsuits in federal district court in Connecticut since last December aren't outliers.
In contrast, children without legal representation received removal orders at more than twice the rate (47%) of children with legal representation (21%)," the Congressional Research Service found.
text:
A system of shelters and foster care facilities meant to hold immigrant children in federal custody for short periods before the government can release them to family has been plagued by delays, with a child in Connecticut as young as five spending months cut off from their loved ones, a CT Insider investigation found.

The federal government held more than two dozen children who were in the country illegally in such facilities here in Connecticut on an average day last spring, sources familiar with the facilities who are not authorized to speak publicly about the federally-controlled programs say. Some of those children are in shelters, others sleeping in the homes of foster parents who are strangers when they first arrive.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nationally, federal data shows these children waited an average of 205 days in May to be freed to their families, up from 29 days five years ago compared to that same period. That surge followed the administration of President Donald Trump adding new vetting requirements for the parents and relatives trying to get these children released.

In six Connecticut cases — including 5-year-old Camila, held 118 days, and 12-year-old Jean, held 505 — the way out was expedited with a lawsuit. A federal judge in Connecticut has ruled in two of the cases the extended detentions were illegal.

The federal government has said publicly that the changes behind those delays are meant to protect children, not punish them. Since last year, the government has required more extensive vetting before releasing a child to a sponsor — mandatory DNA testing, expanded background checks and home inspections — and began sharing information about children's families with ICE, a practice the previous administration had blocked to keep relatives from fearing to come forward. The agency has said it has to "front-load" child safety checks rather than prioritizing speed. The White House and its Office of Refugee Resettlement has not returned messages seeking comment for the CT Insider investigation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

CT Insider Logo

Take control of your search results

Make CT Insider a preferred source on Google to see more of our journalism when you search.

Add Preferred Source

Connecticut can't force the federal government to release detained immigrant children faster, although its Democratic leaders would want to.

"This is child abuse," U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, a Democrat from New Haven, stated in a press release following CT Insider's investigation this past week. “President Trump and Stephen Miller were the architects behind the zero-tolerance family separation policy during the first Trump administration. They are intent on continuing this inhumane policy, just in a new form. We cannot allow this. I am demanding answers and will seek a full accounting of every child still needlessly detained. The administration must reunite these children with their families without delay."

Control of the immigration system largely falls with the federal government — but Connecticut's leaders aren't powerless, either. So far, though, the state's response to the Trump Administration's broad immigration changes have focused mostly on pressuring Washington to change course and shielding immigrants in Connecticut as much as possible from those changes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Here are five changes advocates say could alter the system.

Two — faster federal processing and guaranteed legal representation — could actually shorten how long a child stays in custody. The first is up to lawmakers in Washington, D.C. The second is within the state's reach, if lawmakers choose to fund it. The remaining three are also things state lawmakers or officials could do on their own. They wouldn't speed anyone's release, but it could make the wait itself less damaging. They include requiring every program that holds these immigrant children to be licensed, keeping them on track in school by ensuring students get credit towards graduation for the courses they take while in custody and checking in after release to make sure they're safe.

Faster processing

Nothing would cut a child's time in custody faster than the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement moving through applications at the pace it historically has. A review of federal data dating back to 2015 shows that the current stay is three times higher than the previous peak over that time.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Federal regulations already require the office to decide on a parent or guardian's application within 10 days once it is deemed complete — but the agency controls when an application counts as "complete" and can keep adding requirements before that clock starts.

In some of the cases CT Insider reviewed, parents weren't given an application to fill out for months after their child entered custody. There were also cases where it took months to schedule DNA tests — despite federal field guidance that says it should take officials five to seven days to schedule a test once they decide it's needed — and cases where officials required home inspections that attorneys for the children say no federal law, regulation or field guidance requires.

Under the administration of President Joe Biden, the federal government released more than 1,000 immigrant children a year to sponsors living in Connecticut, federal data shows. Last year, 200 children were released. Through the first half of this year, only seven. During Trump's first term in office, roughly 500 children were released to sponsors in Connecticut each year.

If the government believes more DNA tests and home inspections are necessary, nothing stops it from running that vetting on fixed deadlines instead of an open-ended one. There is some leeway for more complicated cases, although advocates argue the federal government is taking advantage of that process.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"It's within ORR's control to comply with its own regulations that require the expeditious consideration and processing of sponsorship applications. What we have seen is a pattern of actions by ORR intended to delay the release of children," said Sabrina Tavi, an attorney at the Center for Children's Advocacy who represents Camila and other immigrant children. "There is no excuse for the excessive delays of months that we have seen ORR take to order these tests and studies. ... . ORR imposes hurdle after hurdle, in a manner that causes unreasonable delays, each time dashing a child's hope of being reunified with their family and further inflicting trauma."

The White House and ORR did not respond to questions about whether they think these months-long delays are appropriate or what, if anything, they are doing to shorten them.

In a sworn declaration filed in one Connecticut case, Toby Biswas, ORR’s assistant deputy director for policy, wrote that the agency has no way to monitor children after they’re released or take them back if a sponsor poses a risk, unlike law enforcement or state child welfare agencies.

The federal government has pointed to alleged instances of human trafficking and child abuse to justify its more stringent vetting policies — though CT Insider has found apparent discrepancies with at least some of those claims.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“ORR must front-load child safety considerations in its identity verification and sponsor-vetting policies," Biswas wrote in a Connecticut court filing, defending the government holding a 12 year old Jean for over 500 days.

Given that priority to "front-load" safety checks over release speed and its broader push toward voluntary departures, attorneys and advocates interviewed by CT Insider do not expect things to change without more lawsuits.

Provide children with lawyers

Legal aid for these children isn't new — it traces back to a legal settlement in 1997 that set minimum standards for how the government treats immigrant children in custody and a federal law passed in 2008 that directs the federal government to ensure children have counsel "to the greatest extent practicable." Together, the two have paved the way for two decades of federally-funded legal representation for unaccompanied children — the same funding stream the Trump administration is working to unwind.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The lawyers who sued to bring Camila home worked for free, as did the attorneys in most of the other cases CT Insider reviewed.

But filing a habeas lawsuit to challenge the detention of a child, or to help with an immigration case, takes an attorney with the time, willingness and expertise to take on a labor-intensive fight, advocates say — which is why many families never get one.

"It's always been a challenge because on one hand you have nonprofit attorneys who are tapped out — and before the current crisis, people were tapped out," said Constanza Segovia, director of Hartford Deportation Defense, an immigrant-led organization that tries to help immigrants find attorneys and raise funds to cover legal costs. "And then on the other hand, if you go to the private sector, it's so expensive that it's just unattainable for a ton of people."

The six children whose lawyers filed lawsuits in federal district court in Connecticut since last December aren't outliers. They're illustrative of a larger pattern of children lingering in federal custody with no legal help to challenge a detention at all, experts and attorneys say.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Many of those children also lack representation in immigration court, where the government is often seeking to remove them from the country. Only 51% of unaccompanied children had a lawyer at any point in their case, and representation declined almost every year during the first Trump presidency, according to a analysis of federal immigration court records from 2009 through March 2023 by University of Chicago sociologist Chiara Galli.

"Children who were not represented by an attorney were far more likely to be ordered deported," her research found.

Congressional researchers in 2024 also reported drastic outcomes for those who do not have an attorney.

"Outcomes were considerably different for those with legal representation compared to those without representation. Of the children with legal representation, 7.2% received immigration relief; of those without legal representation, the figure was 0.3%. In contrast, children without legal representation received removal orders at more than twice the rate (47%) of children with legal representation (21%)," the Congressional Research Service found.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Unlike faster processing, this fix doesn't require lawmakers in Washington, D.C. to act — in Connecticut, a foundation, or a legal aid group could fund attorneys for every child in ORR custody on its own. But attorneys and advocates caution that funding alone wouldn't guarantee every child gets help: There simply aren't enough immigration attorneys able to take these labor-intensive cases. Meeting the representation needs of all unaccompanied children would require nearly a fourfold increase in the number of free and low-cost attorneys nationwide, research published last year in the Journal on Migration and Human Security found.

Some families are too afraid of drawing the government's attention to pursue one, even with a lawyer available for free.

"It's become a lot more of a minefield than it used to be," said Segovia.

Last year, the administration of President Donald Trump changed federal regulations to begin sharing information with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement about children’s families that had long been shielded — a wall meant to ensure relatives weren’t afraid to come forward — and ICE used it to locate family members for arrest.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

"Access to legal counsel for these children is the bulwark against many of the exact dangers that ORR claims its new requirements are aimed at preventing," said Tavi, the lawyer for several of the children who were lingering in federal custody in Connecticut programs. "The attorneys representing these children are often the only independent check on the government, who see the conditions the children are in and advocate for their rights. Taking away funding for legal counsel leaves these children unprotected and invisible."

Require state licensing

As of mid-June, there were three programs in the state that had active contracts with the federal government to care for these children — one in New Haven, one in Greenwich and one in Groton.

Two of the three — Groton and Greenwich — are licensed by the state's Department of Children and Families (DCF), which means the state can inspect their classrooms, staffing and living conditions. The New Haven program, where Camila spent her days in a converted office building fitted with classrooms, is not licensed by the state at all — no state agency inspects or monitors it, or the foster homes where children like Camila sleep at night.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Licensing wouldn't speed up the process, but it would give the state the same oversight it already has at the other two programs — the kind that, at the Groton shelter, had already flagged growing lengths of stay as a problem before Camila was ever detained.

Some advocates, however, caution that pushing state-level fixes too hard could backfire and the federal government would simply stop placing children in the state altogether — sending them instead to states with even less access to counsel and less oversight.

"While state oversight is always important, the problem is not with the contracted facilities here in Connecticut who are providing care to these children and do not have control over the sponsorship process. The issue is that children are being detained for unconscionable periods of time despite having available, qualified sponsors, and facilities like the ones Camila was held in are intended to be short-term. Many of them are not set up to provide long-term care," said Tavi.

ORR did not directly answer whether any state agency licenses or inspects the New Haven facility where Camila spent her days. Instead, the agency described a general policy: its providers must be licensed by a state agency, or, where state licensing isn't available, meet state requirements that ORR says it monitors itself — including background checks and mandated reporter training.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In practice, that federal backstop hasn't held up. In June, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' inspector general reported that in Texas and Florida — the two states that stopped licensing immigrant-children providers — the agency completed 176 of 256 required monitoring visits over three years. Because those visits are how the federal government verifies that providers ran mandatory background checks, the watchdog couldn't confirm that people hired to care for children had cleared criminal and child-abuse screening. Connecticut wasn't part of that review — but it's the same self-monitoring arrangement ORR says covers New Haven now.

Fix the education gap for kids

As the average stay now stretches past six months, some children are falling behind, both academically and on the credits they need to graduate high school, lawyers representing children in the cases CT Insider reviewed allege.

Camila attended class alone, the only student in her age group at the New Haven facility. Miguel, 14, sat in lessons built for children as young as 11.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

And none of that coursework necessarily transfers to whatever school a child enrolls in after release.

Fixing that isn't fully within the state Department of Education's reach, either. The programs teaching these children aren't public schools — they're privately run and federally contracted, which means the state doesn't control their curriculum or accreditation. Getting a child credit that a future school will actually accept depends on those programs seeking outside accreditation on their own, something nothing currently requires them to do since the extended stays are a new issue.

The cost isn't abstract: a teenager held eight months into a school year can lose the credits needed to graduate on schedule, and a 5-year-old isolated from peers loses something a shelter classroom can't replace.

Add post-release check-ins

Once a child leaves federal custody, ORR officials say they have no way to take them back if a sponsor poses a risk — a point the agency itself has made in court filings defending its decision to "front load" vetting rules.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

ORR does conduct post-release calls and home visits, but immigrant families frequently don't answer or engage, afraid that contact will be used to deport them.

The state doesn't have to rely on the federal government's version of a check-in. A state-run post-release check-in — confirming a child is enrolled in school, still has a lawyer for the immigration case that isn't over and isn't at risk of trafficking or exploitation — would not require federal cooperation and could come from a source families might trust more than the same agency that just held their child for months.

California is doing just that. The Children’s Holistic Immigration Representation Project, or CHIRP, pairs lawyers and social workers together to work with unaccompanied children once they're released from ORR — providing them with legal representation, trauma-informed counseling, social services and community support.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

CHIRP is run by the Acacia Center for Justice, a nonprofit that also holds the national contract to provide legal services for children in ORR custody. But it relies on a bevy of service providers across the state. The program launched in the fall of 2022 as a two-year pilot program. California Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers recently renewed its funding in their 2026 – 2027 budget.

A 2024 evaluation by Acacia found that CHIRP “improved the quality of services provided to unaccompanied children, supported their integration into communities, and more effectively connected them to services and trusted adults that can support their overall well-being.”

text:
New guidance distributed to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents across the country in recent days said that the FBI will no longer investigate confrontations that officers have with protesters or people who are subjected to immigration enforcement—leaving the agency to investigate its own violent encounters with the public following at least two recent killings by ICE agents.

The guidance pertained to claims of assault against Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officers, but FBI investigations have gathered evidence that implicated agents themselves after they claimed to have been attacked.

According to the message sent to ICE officers, Homeland Security Investigations, which operates under ICE, would begin examining incidents in which an agent claimed they were assaulted.

HSI does not have jurisdiction to investigate allegations of civil rights allegations, so in cases in which a confrontation escalates to a use of force by an officer, the unit would be unlikely to investigate whether the agent violated the victim's rights, The New York Times reported.

"The fox is guarding the hen house," said American Immigration Council senior fellow Aaron Reichlin-Melnick of the reported change.

Despite the guidance that was circulated to agents, the US Department of Justice, which oversees the FBI, released a joint statement with DHS denying that the change would take place.

“The relationship between DHS and DOJ in investigating assault on federal officer cases has not changed, and FBI will continue to investigate in accordance with agency policy,” the statement said. “This administration has been clear, anyone who assaults law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

According to a New York Times investigation, the Trump administration filed charges against more than 550 people who it said assaulted federal immigration officers. More than 400 of the cases had been resolved, and in nearly half of them, charges of assault had been thrown out or withdrawn, or the defendants had been acquitted.

As it's filed such charges, the Trump administration has frequently repeated its assertion that federal agents are regularly facing violent attacks from the public—including in cases in which agents have killed US citizens and immigrants, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and earlier this month, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

The reported change was also made public less than a week after an ICE agent fatally shot Johan Sebastián Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine.

The moves came after ICE agents shot and killed two people in separate traffic stops. An agent shot Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7. The Department of Homeland Security said Salgado Araujo “weaponized his vehicle,” a statement his family has disputed.

Trending

Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian national, was shot and killed while in his car by an ICE agent in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13. DHS said in a statement that the agent who shot him was “fearing for public safety” but did not explain more.

Homan said Sunday that the rollout of body cameras for ICE agents was delayed because

Democrats blocked funding for immigration enforcement agencies during the 76-day partial government shutdown this year.

“Everybody in ICE would have a camera now if the government wasn’t shut down by Democratic members of Congress,” Homan said. “There was money in that bill that they held up.”

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington state, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, disputed the contention that the shutdown played any role in outfitting agents with body cameras. A Republican tax and spending bill passed in 2025 included nearly $30 billion for ICE.

“This administration instead blew tax dollars on private jets and new souped-up, gold-coated SUVs that the agency cannot even use,” Murray told HuffPost in a statement last week. “The idea that Democrats are to blame for the Trump administration’s failure to deploy body cameras to the field and to protect people from out-of-control agents that they have failed to properly train is completely absurd.”

"Because they created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court."
text:
The Justice Department is asking a never-before-used federal court to remove an unnamed noncitizen, the first use of a 30-year-old process that could give President Trump a new tool for his deportation agenda.

Why it matters: If the Justice Department wins, it could remove people it links to terrorism while keeping much of its evidence secret.

A loss could show why this court sat idle for 30 years: The law may demand more than the government wants to provide.

Driving the news: The DOJ filed the first application in the Alien Terrorist Removal Court's history last Wednesday.

The one-page filing does not name the person, the alleged conduct or the part of the anti-terrorism law the department cited. News site Court Watch first reported the filing.

Chief Judge Joan N. Ericksen, who heard arguments Thursday, questioned the connection between the person's alleged actions and the law.

She ordered the government to provide more facts and legal analysis by Wednesday.

The White House referred requests for comment to the Justice Department, which did not respond.

How it works: The law sets up two stages: one private and the other public.

In private, one judge decides if there is probable cause.

At the public hearing, DOJ must show it is more likely than not that the person meets the law's definition of an "alien terrorist."

Even in public, the person facing removal and the public don't have the right to see classified evidence, but the DOJ must provide an unclassified summary.

Context: Congress created the five-judge court in 1996 for cases when ordinary immigration proceedings could expose classified information and threaten national security.

The definition of a terrorist covers noncitizens who carried out or are likely to carry out terrorist activity. It also includes those who incite or endorse terrorism, represent or belong to certain terrorist groups, or receive military-type training from them.

Normal federal evidence rules don't apply. The law explicitly allows the U.S. to use illegally obtained evidence.

Flashback: The DOJ considered 100 possible cases by 2000 and rejected all of them, according to a 9/11 Commission staff report.

Officials found ordinary immigration charges sufficient, the report says.

Between the lines: Trump invoked the Alien Enemies Act in 2025 to remove Venezuelans his administration accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua. The Supreme Court ruled that people targeted under that law must receive notice and a chance to challenge their removal.

During that litigation, Chief Judge James Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia pointed DOJ to the Alien Terrorist Removal Court.

"Congress has an answer for us, doesn't it?" Boasberg said. "Because they created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court."

Reality check: While the court offers a new route for deportations, it seems ill-equipped to work en masse.

To win deportation, all cases must go through senior DOJ approval, a judge's review and a full hearing.

What's next: DOJ's supplemental filing is due Wednesday.

title: Hundreds protest ICE operations in Houston, demand justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo
authors: Bianca Seward, Michael Adkison, Michael Hagerty, Kyle McClenagan
description:
RELATED: ‘That's my hero': Houstonians remember Lorenzo Salgado Araujo at funeral, days after ICE shooting Ronaldo said the family laid their father to rest Saturday.
A public vigil and celebration of Salgado Araujo's life was held Thursday.
Salgado Araujo was fatally shot by ICE agents during what the agency called a "targeted enforcement operation."
The Department of Homeland Security later confirmed Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation.
The three other men traveling with Salgado Araujo dispute the account of ICE agents and said the agent fired immediately upon opening the passenger door of Salgado Araujo's white van.
text:
Hundreds of protestors gathered in Ervan Chew Park Sunday afternoon in the Montrose neighborhood to demand transparency and accountability for the killing of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was shot and killed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents on July 7.

Battling the brutal heat and humidity, protest organizers called off the planned march just thirty minutes before it was scheduled to begin.

The protest — organized by Immigration Youth Texas, the Houston Chapter of the Party for Socialism and Liberation and dozens of other organizations — started just after noon. Stephanie Padilla with Immigration Youth Texas said she made the call to stop the march after a few people at the pre-march rally overheated. Temperatures remained in the mid-nineties for the afternoon.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Hundreds stayed at the park, the march's starting point, listening to speeches from organizers about how to support their movement to demand changes to Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations. The crowd briefly took over the bridge on Dunlavy St., crossing over the Southwest Freeway and closing down the street.

Two of Salgado Araujo's sons — Ronaldo and Lorenzo Jr. — stood on picnic tables and repeated their calls for accountability and transparency.

"We want to continue pressuring the government to allow for a full, transparent, independent investigation," Ronaldo said. "It’s very nice to see so many people, so many people of all backgrounds, races, colors, creeds, religions come together and try to ask for what’s right. Try to ask for the bare minimum, and it's going to be justice."

RELATED: ‘That's my hero': Houstonians remember Lorenzo Salgado Araujo at funeral, days after ICE shooting

Ronaldo said the family laid their father to rest Saturday. A public vigil and celebration of Salgado Araujo's life was held Thursday.

"It’s been extremely hard and even after 11 days of going 100 miles an hour and trying to plan a beautiful celebration for my dad, I know that the fight is not over yet," Ronaldo said. "There’s still a lot to be done."

Salgado Araujo was fatally shot by ICE agents during what the agency called a "targeted enforcement operation." The Department of Homeland Security later confirmed Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation. The agents allege that during the encounter, Salgado Araujo "weaponized" his vehicle and attempted to run over the agent when they fired in "self-defense."

The three other men traveling with Salgado Araujo dispute the account of ICE agents and said the agent fired immediately upon opening the passenger door of Salgado Araujo's white van.

Currently, there are four different investigations into the shooting. The Harris County DA's office has launched an investigation. The Texas Rangers also are investigating at the request of the Houston Police Department, according to Gov. Greg Abbott. The Office of Inspector General for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is conducting its own investigation into the shooting death, according to the FBI, which has said it is investigating a possible assault on a law enforcement officer.

RELATED: ‘They're killing me': Lawyer for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's brother shares his account of fatal shooting by ICE

Mariela Rivera said she came to the protest because she feels "helpless" and hopes the protest influences leaders to make changes.

"In what world is murder or someone not being a citizen a validation of murder?" Rivera asked. "I feel like there’s not much I can do. I’m hoping that when everyone sees this, they think this is not something that us as Americans — a democracy — want."

Continued Calls for Transparency

For Anna Garcia West, Salgado Araujo's death hit close to home. She called his killing by ICE agents a human rights issue.

"Lorenzo reminds me of my dad and how I came to be here," Garcia West said. "My father came looking for a better life. It just really strikes me that his sons would have to be without a dad and that now their mom is a widow. It's just something that feels very personal."

Salgado Araujo's death sparked outrage in communities throughout the city. Protesters swarmed Houston City Hall last Tuesday, and nearly 100 people spoke directly to city council members and the mayor, demanding changes to ICE operations and calling for accountability and transparency.

RELATED: Texas Rangers will investigate ICE shooting in Houston. Here's what that means

Across the country, arrests and deportations have surged during the second term of President Donald Trump.

Sasha Monterroso urged the city council to launch its own independent investigation of the shooting death — one of several across the country during the last two years at the hands of (ICE).

“Justice cannot depend on who pulled the trigger,” Monterroso said Tuesday. “Accountability cannot disappear because a federal badge was involved. An independent investigation is not an attack on the law enforcement. It is a commitment to transparency, accountability, and the principle that no one is above scrutiny.”

authors: Diana Novak Jones, The Christian Science Monitor
description:
In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday.
Mr. Homan’s comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six ​days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month.
There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.
Mr. Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures.
The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston, ​and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents’ lack of body cameras.

In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday.

“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action,” Mr. Homan said on the “Fox & Friends Weekend” program.

Mr. Homan’s comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six ​days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.

In a separate interview on CBS’ “Face the Nation” show, Mr. Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

“The cameras have been purchased right now,” Mr. Homan said. “They’re training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide.”

Traffic stops resume

The agency’s tactics came under ⁠renewed public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on July 13 killed a driver from Colombia in the coastal Maine town of Biddeford, about 15 miles south of Portland. Six ​days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot a Mexican national.

Mr. Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Mr. Homan’s comments, U.S. President ​Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.

The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston, ​and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents’ lack of body cameras.

ICE launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed cameras to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C.

The Trump administration moved last year to slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut funding by 75%, Reuters reported in January.

In February, after the killing of two U.S. citizens during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota, then U.S. Department of Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem said the body camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide “as funding is available.”

At least seven people have been shot dead during federal immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump launched mass deportations after returning to office following campaign promises of an immigration crackdown.

(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones; Editing by Sergio Non and Chizu Nomiyama )

title: What The Pending $100000 H-1B Fee Litigation Means For Employers And Foreign Nationals
authors: Tetiana P.  Lendiel, Tetiana P. Lendiel

text:
Recent weeks have provided a reminder of just how quickly the U.S. immigration landscape can change.

In early June 2026, a federal court decision struck down the $100,000 fee imposed on certain H-1B petitions. Within days, however, the federal government appealed the decision and obtained a temporary stay, creating renewed uncertainty about whether the fee would remain in place while the litigation proceeds.

While the legal battle over the fee continues, the broader lesson extends beyond the H-1B program: immigration planning calls for employers and foreign nationals to prepare for continued policy shifts, litigation-driven uncertainty, and changing compliance obligations.

The $100,000 H-1B Fee: A Brief Overview

The $100,000 fee originated from a September 2025 presidential proclamation and applied to certain new H-1B petitions involving beneficiaries outside of the United States who would require consular processing. The stated purpose was to discourage perceived abuse of the H-1B program and protect U.S. workers. On June 8, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts invalidated the fee, concluding that:

The fee functioned as a tax rather than a regulatory filing fee;

The executive branch lacked authority to impose such a tax without congressional approval; and

The implementing agencies exceeded their authority and violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The court vacated the policy in its entirety, providing immediate relief for employers facing additional costs associated with H-1B sponsorship.

Temporary Relief

The federal government quickly appealed the Massachusetts court’s decision, seeking a stay pending review by the First Circuit Court of Appeals. The Circuit Court granted a temporary stay, effectively allowing the government to continue enforcing the fee while the appellate process unfolds.

As a result, employers face uncertainty regarding filing strategies, workforce planning, and immigration budgets. A policy that appeared invalid one week was back in effect the next.

This sequence of events highlights a recurring trend in today’s immigration environment: policy developments often do not end with a district court ruling. Appeals, injunctions, stays, and conflicting court decisions sometimes alter the practical impact of a decision within days.

For employers, the litigation illustrates the potential benefits of building flexibility into immigration budgets, hiring timelines, and global mobility planning.

Considerations for Employers

Employers should evaluate whether particular H-1B filings may be affected by the fee, especially where the beneficiary is outside the United States or the petition requires consular notification. At the same time, companies may wish to avoid making long-term workforce decisions based solely on a single court ruling or headline. Appeals, stays, and further agency action may change the practical effect of a decision quickly.

Organizations that rely on temporary visa programs may wish to monitor litigation developments and assess budget exposure for affected cases.

Potential Implications for Foreign Nationals

For foreign nationals, the case underscores the potential benefits of maintaining flexibility and planning. Some nonimmigrant visa holders depend on a series of immigration benefits — petition approvals, visa appointments, extensions, status maintenance, and travel authorization — to remain in and work in the United States. Policy changes affecting any one of those stages may create delays and uncertainty.

The recent litigation involving both the H-1B fee and other challenged immigration policies demonstrates that even seemingly favorable court rulings may not produce long-term certainty. Appeals may prolong uncertainty for months or even years.

One question raised by the government’s decision to appeal is why further litigation is necessary if the fee was originally implemented for a limited period and is reportedly scheduled to expire in September 2026. While the government has not publicly articulated all of its reasons, the appeal may reflect broader institutional interests that extend beyond the collection of the fee itself. For example, the administration may seek to preserve the underlying legal authority asserted in the presidential proclamation, avoid creating judicial precedent that could limit future immigration-related actions, or maintain the ability to collect the fee during the remaining period in which it is authorized. Whatever its motivation, the government’s appeal may signal that it considers the legal issues important notwithstanding the fee’s potentially limited remaining lifespan.

Looking Ahead

Further appellate review — and, potentially, additional litigation — may determine the fate of the $100,000 H-1B fee. For now, employers and foreign nationals should monitor developments and consider seeking case-specific immigration guidance before making filing, hiring, budgeting, or travel decisions.

Regardless of its outcome, the litigation surrounding the H-1B fee highlights a broader reality of modern immigration practice: policy shifts can occur rapidly, and immigration planning may benefit from proactive strategies rather than reactive responses.

text:
For women on temporary visas experiencing domestic and family violence (DFV) in Australia, their perpetrators are often also their visa sponsors.

And returning to their home countries is usually unthinkable, as many are terrified of being separated from their Australian children, or they know they will face stigma or abuse over the ended relationship.

The Department of Home Affairs has family violence provisions under the Migration Act, but the application asks for proof the relationship was "genuine" via documents that usually do not exist.

Warning: This story includes details of domestic and family violence.

For migrant mother Sophia, which is a name she has chosen to protect her identity, the abuse perpetrated by her then-husband and visa sponsor included physical, verbal and sexual abuse.

She also survived coercive control and was not permitted to leave the house, learn English or access money.

"He controlled my communication and isolated me.

"He said, 'If you could contact your sister, if you share anything to your sister … I will deport you'."

Sophia said she resorted to secretly collecting cans from bins to exchange for 10 cents each so she could buy food for her child.

When the relationship ended, she was eventually supported by Settlement Services International to apply for the Home Affairs family violence provisions.

Sophia was required to provide proof her relationship was "genuine" through joint bills, bank accounts, leases, mortgages, or even invitations addressed to the couple.

She had access to none of those things due to the coercive control.

Sophia applied for the provisions in 2023 and is still waiting.

'Pillars of the relationship'

Immigration Advice and Rights Centre senior solicitor Kristie Mellor said the department had its process backwards.

"They look at what they call the pillars of the relationship, which includes financial aspects of the relationship, the nature of the household, the social aspects of the relationship, and the nature of the couple's commitment to each other," she said.

The department's process means it must decide whether the relationship was "genuine" before assessing claims of DFV.

Ms Mellor said the sequence was highly problematic with many clients "falling down at the first step".

"You'd usually be looking at joint bank accounts or things to show they've pooled their finances as a couple. [But] where a client's experienced financial abuse, for example, those documents are essentially impossible."

She said if the department were to consider DFV evidence first, then due to the nature of the incidents occurring within an intimate partnership, it could then "assume the relationship is genuine".

Ms Mellor said the provisions were "really tricky to navigate without legal assistance", and she feared for those who could not get support.

'We're sorry, you have to go home'

Legal Aid ACT lawyer Jessica Liao said the provisions excluded swathes of temporary visa holders.

Ms Liao said migrants who were secondary applicants to their partner's student visa were among those excluded.

"So if the person experiences family violence in that situation, then there's no way to access those protections," she said.

"And Canberra's a big student town," her colleague, Legal Aid ACT lawyer Lyn Payne, said.

"There are a lot of people here, international students, and we do see, unfortunately, quite a lot of women who are dependent on their husband's student visa. So the husband's here studying, the wife has come, sometimes there's children, and there's family violence.

"All they can do if they want to leave the violent relationship, is to leave the country."

Ms Payne said this was problematic as a partner's student visa had the potential to lead to permanent skills-based visas, which could compel a victim-survivor to stay in an unsafe relationship for immigration security.

When Ms Payne was asked whether she believed the omission of some temporary visas from the provisions was an oversight, she disagreed.

Status unknown

Ms Liao said many clients had little knowledge about their immigration status.

"We've even seen people who've come from domestic violence, leave relationships with violence and not realise what visa they were holding," she said.

"Even people who are permanent residents, not knowing that they were permanent residents and they could actually leave those relationships without the threat of being sent back or needing to report to the Department of Home Affairs."

It is those situations, similar to her own, that have prompted Sophia to share this message with new migrants:

Perpetrators ask friends to lie

Professor of Criminology Marie Segrave has researched temporary migration and DFV.

She said perpetrators who were aware of the department's "genuine" relationship test were able to derail it by creating "suspicion".

"Perpetrators try to ensure that victims aren't on the lease, that they don't have a shared bank account, that they're basically in control of every aspect of their lives," Professor Segrave said.

"They can also demand payment for a visa so that they can say, 'No this person basically was paying me to stay in the country'.

"But it was, in fact, part of the pattern of coercion that they were trying to get more money from the victim and trying to control the victim through this creation of a debt."

Professor Segrave said that as part of the government's national plan to end violence against women and children, "this would be a major area of reform that would be transformative".

'Unprecedented' visa cancellations

In a statement, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he had expanded the number of visa classes that could access assistance for domestic and family violence, "and lowered the barrier to accessing assistance".

"The character test allows the government to cancel the visa of anyone who doesn't meet the standards of our community, and we can use those powers to protect people in our community."

In a separate statement, a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said there were also processes in place to stop known perpetrators from sponsoring further partner visas.

"Any future visa applications by a sponsor who has previously been associated with an application granted under the FVPs [family violence provisions] would be appropriately scrutinised by the department," the spokesperson said.

"Limitations apply to the number of partner visas an individual can sponsor", the spokesperson said, including a lifetime limit of two.

text:
The Trump administration has filed a first-ever petition to a secretive and dormant court created 30 years ago to consider government requests to deport “alien terrorists” from the United States.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was established in 1996 but had never received a petition until Wednesday, when the Justice Department filed an application seeking the removal of an individual whose name is withheld from the single-page document posted on the court’s website.

The chief judge of the five-member court, Joan Ericksen, said in a written response to the petition that a hearing was held Thursday during which the court had “questions about the nexus that the government alleges between the actions of the respondent and the specific sections and subsections it invokes with respect to those actions.”

“The answers persuaded the Court that the Government could benefit from the opportunity for more thoughtful consideration,” wrote Ericksen, a federal judge in Minnesota.

She directed the Justice Department to provide more information by Wednesday.

The court’s authorities emerged from the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, which permits the attorney general to file under seal applications for the deportation of a suspected “alien terrorist.” If an application is granted, the court must hold a public hearing at which the government has the burden to prove that the individual satisfies that definition. Applications must be approved by the attorney general or deputy attorney general.

Federal law says that an individual could qualify as an “alien terrorist” by, among other factors, having “engaged in a terrorist activity,” endorsing or espousing terrorist activities and by belonging to a political or social group that encourages terrorist activity.

The court has been dormant since its creation, having received — until last week — no applications and conducting no hearings, according to a summary posted on the Federal Judicial Center website. It comprises five judges selected by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.

The Trump administration has moved aggressively over the last year to carry out deportations, including invoking a 1798 wartime law, the Alien Enemies Act, to remove Venezuelan migrants who officials accuse of being part of a terrorist gang. During a hearing in that case last year, the Washington judge presiding over it, James Boasberg, indicated that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court would be the natural forum to consider a request for deportation on national security grounds.

“In fact, Congress has an answer for us, doesn’t it? Because they created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court,” he said. “So if there’s a national security concern with having these hearings ... you can always go to the ATRC, which would be a first, but that’s what it’s there for, right?”

The petition was first reported by Court Watch, an independent news site.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents recently have been told that the FBI will no longer investigate claims of assault against the federal officers, according to a report by The New York Times.

On Thursday, FBI managers received written notice of the change, sources told the Times, and some ICE agents throughout the country were informed by their FBI counterparts.

In incidents where ICE agents have been involved in fatal shootings, the FBI under the Trump administration has been tasked with determining whether the agents were assaulted before opening fire. But evidence revealed during those investigations could later be used in civil rights investigations or prosecutions against ICE agents.

The new guidance would likely mean Homeland Security Investigations, an arm of ICE, would investigate such assault claims by their own agents, according to the Times. Allowing DHS to handle those investigations could lead to less accountability for immigration agents, sources told the NYT.

Since DHS does not have the jurisdiction to investigate civil rights violations, the policy change could lessen the likelihood that ICE agents who shoot unarmed people would be investigated for breaking federal law.

The Department of Justice and the DHS have both denied that any change in oversight has taken place.

"The Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security are partners in addressing crime and upholding the rule of law, while securing the safety and security of American communities," the DHS and DOJ said in a joint statement provided to CNBC.

"The relationship between DHS and DOJ in investigating assault on federal officer cases has not changed, and FBI will continue to investigate in accordance with agency policy."

The purported change in oversight comes just days after an ICE agent shot and killed a Colombian man, Joan Sebastian Guerrero, in Biddeford, Maine. He was at least the seventh person shot by ICE agents since January 2025, and the second person just this month after an agent shot and killed Mexican immigrant Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston on July 7.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested an Alaska state attorney in Anchorage and is holding him in an ICE detention facility in Washington state, according to an agency spokesperson.

Shucheng Yang, a 32-year-old Chinese national, was arrested in Anchorage on July 10.

“Yang violated the terms of his admission and is a deportable alien,” said Jason Chudy, an ICE Public Affairs officer, by email on Thursday. He said Yang is currently detained in the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington, pending immigration proceedings.

Yang is an attorney with the Alaska Department of Law’s labor, business and corporations section, according to the state employee database. Yang was admitted to the Alaska Bar Association and licensed to practice law in the state in June 2025. A spokesperson for the department declined to respond to questions about his immigration status, employment status or work authorization when hired, saying the department does not comment on personnel matters.

Chudy declined to say how Yang violated the terms of admission into the country. “To be clear, work authorization does NOT confer legal status in the United States,” he said in the email.

He referred further questions about Yang’s work authorization to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. A spokesperson for USCIS referred the question back to ICE, and said the agency does not comment on individual immigration cases.

The state requires applicants to self-disclose their employment eligibility and work authorization through the I-9 verification process during hiring, according to the Alaska Department of Administration, as reported by Alaska News Source.

There are no state criminal charges against Yang, according to court records. Yang pleaded no contest on June 26 for a speeding citation.

A spokesperson for the Municipality of Anchorage confirmed the Anchorage Police Department issued the traffic ticket on April 25. “They have had no other interaction with Mr. Yang since April,” said Nora Morse, communications director for the municipality, by email on Thursday.

“The Anchorage Police Department does not ask for someone’s immigration status as part of a routine traffic stop,” Morse said.

A spokesperson for the ACLU of Alaska said they were trying to get in touch with Yang’s attorney, and had no other information on his case.

The Alaska Department of Corrections contracts with ICE to hold detainees in Alaska under an agreement with the U.S. Marshals. A spokesperson confirmed that Yang was detained in Alaska for two days after his arrest until he was transferred on July 12.

DOC has held 17 people arrested by ICE since June 1, and 73 people since the beginning of the calendar year, according to spokesperson Betsy Holley on Thursday.

text:
US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, said Tom Homan, the Trump administration “border czar”, on Sunday. The action comes as the agency is under renewed scrutiny after ICE officers fatally shot two men earlier this month.

“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the ⁠officers saw when they took that action,” Homan said on the Fox & Friends Weekend program.

Homan’s comments come after federal ​immigration agents fatally shot two men six days ‌apart during traffic stops in ‌Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.

In a ‌separate interview on CBS’s Face the Nation show, Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

“The cameras have been purchased right now,” Homan said. “They’re training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide.”

The immigration agency’s extreme tactics have once again come under public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on 13 July killed Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a driver from Colombia, in the coastal Maine ‌city of Biddeford, about 15 miles (24km) south of Portland. Six days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national.

Salgado, who was not the intended target of the ICE officers, was driving his construction crew to a job site when he was pursued and stopped. Salgado had no criminal history, had lived in the US for 35 years and was close to obtaining legal status, his family has said.

Less than a week later, ICE agents shot and killed Durán during another traffic stop. As with Salgado, Durán was not the target of an operation. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed officers feared for their safety. Immigrant rights activists have said Durán was authorized to work in the US and had a social security number.

Homan said last week the ​agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Homan’s comments, Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.

The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents’ lack of body cameras.

ICE launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed ⁠cameras to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia and Washington DC. The Trump ​administration moved last year to ​slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut ​funding by 75%, Reuters reported in January.

In February, after the killing of two US ​citizens during an immigration crackdown ‌in Minnesota, Kristi Noem, then the DHS chief, said the body-camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide “as funding is available”.

The killing of Durán was the 11th fatal shooting by federal immigration officials since Trump’s second term began, including the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, according to a Guardian review of public reports.

FBI agents will no longer be investigating confrontations with ICE agents, a New York Times report said, citing people briefed on the decision. They said written notice had been sent on Thursday of this decision. Previously, these investigation cases could yield information that could be used to prosecute ICE agents involved in violent encounters.

Dani Anguiano contributed reporting

text:
Alim Garipov, an 18-year-old student from Bellaire High School, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Friday night at William P. Hobby Airport. ICE alleges that Garipov overstayed his visa, while his supporters say he has a pending asylum case.

"Alim Garipov, was 'forcefully' arrested by ICE at Hobby Airport," Elizabeth Chapman Sun, a Bellaire High School teacher, posted to Facebook on Saturday. "He has been in the country legally for five years and has a pending asylum case [from Russia]."

"Is there anyone who knows how we can help?" Chapman Sun wrote. "He is the kindest, most sensitive boy. He started a Russian Culture Club at Bellaire and did the sweetest celebration for International Women's Day. He has worked so, so hard to learn English."

"He is a kid. He has done everything right and more. He was afraid of making grammar mistakes in class; I'm sure being thrown around like a dangerous criminal is terrifying to him," she wrote.

The case has also drawn the attention of U.S. Rep. Lizzie Fletcher, who represents the state's 7th Congressional District in Greater Houston. Fletcher addressed Garipov's detention in a Facebook post Saturday.

"Thank you to the many people who have reached out to me today and shared your concerns about reports of a TX07 student detained at Hobby Airport," Fletcher said. "I am working with his family and am in touch with the federal agencies involved. My team and I will do all we can to help."

As community members continued advocating for Garipov, ICE offered a different account of his immigration status. On Saturday night, a spokesperson confirmed that Garipov was detained Friday, alleging that he had overstayed his visa.

"Garipov was admitted into the U.S. May 7, 2022, as a non-immigrant with permission to remain in the country no later than Nov. 6, 2022, but he failed to depart," the spokesperson wrote, adding that the Trump administration considers stricter immigration enforcement necessary to protect national security and public safety.

"If a person enters our country illegally, they are subject to detention or deportation. Each illegal alien receives due process," the spokesperson wrote. "Receiving a 'work permit' does NOT confer any form of lawful status or prevent ICE from arresting or deporting an illegal alien from the country."

A Bay Area family was flying home to San Francisco International Airport with lingering fears of detainment after a viral video showed a United Airlines employee threatening to call immigration authorities on them during a ticketing dispute.

Julio Varela of San Ramon said neither the airport nor United Airlines has contacted his family of four to assure them they will not be detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) upon their return from Montreal Saturday night.

"I don’t even know what’s going to happen when I get back to San Francisco," Varela said from the Montreal airport prior to his flight. "I don’t know what’s gonna happen when I get back."

The incident occurred July 14 at the United Airlines counter at SFO as the family was trying to leave for a trip to Canada. Varela said a customer service representative refused to help fix an issue with his daughter’s ticket, which had incorrectly listed her last name as her middle name due to an error his wife accidentally made when booking the flight a few months ago.

Varela noted that a different United representative had advised them by phone to arrive at SFO early Tuesday so airport customer service could fix the error. After waiting nearly three hours, Varela said an employee from a United partner airline was close to resolving the issue, but a United worker stepped in and dismissed them.

"She walks over and says, 'What, you’re still here? We already told you we can do this,' and she just starts complaining about it," Varela said. "She said, 'I don’t care. That’s her problem. Take it up with her. I don’t care if you guys fly out today or not.'"

Frustrated by the interaction, Varela pulled out his phone and asked for the employee's name to report her. He said the worker refused to identify herself, pulled out her own phone to start recording, and threatened to call ICE.

In the viral video, the employee can be heard saying, "Maybe we should call ICE on you."

When Varela asked her to repeat the statement, she replied, "Maybe you need to be, because you don’t act like a citizen. Get away."

Varela expressed disbelief over the encounter.

"It infuriated me, because I am a citizen, number one, and for her to threaten me like that with ICE, especially with the state of politics now in America and with what ICE is doing," he said.

The confrontation also escalated physically, according to Varela. After a brief back-and-forth, the video shows the employee's hand reaching toward the camera before Varela's phone goes dark. Varela alleges the employee hit his hand and his phone, constituting an assault.

"When she pushed me, I squeezed it, so then I turned it back on again," he said.

United Airlines issued a brief statement regarding the incident.

"We’re looking into the interaction in this video, but don’t have anything additional to share at this time," the airline said.

The communications director for the employee's union said the organization is aware of the video but has not yet verified its authenticity.

"As depicted, the comments made in the video do not reflect the views or values of the IAM Union," the communications director stated. "Any potential matters arising from this incident will be handled through the appropriate processes established by the collective bargaining agreement."

San Francisco International Airport officials have not responded to requests for comment.

Meanwhile, the Varelas' flight was scheduled to land in San Francisco Saturday night. It was unclear if the family faced further issues at the airport.

In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday.

"They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action," Homan said on the "Fox & Friends Weekend" program.

Homan's comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.

In a separate interview on CBS' "Face the Nation" show, Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.

"The cameras have been purchased right now," Homan said. "They're training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide."

Traffic stops resume

The agency's tactics came under renewed public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on July 13 killed a driver from Colombia in the coastal Maine town of Biddeford, about 15 miles (24 km) south of Portland. Six days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot a Mexican national.

Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Homan's comments, U.S. President Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.

The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents' lack of body cameras.

ICE launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed cameras to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. The Trump administration moved last year to slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut funding by 75%, Reuters reported in January.

In February, after the killing of two U.S. citizens during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota, then U.S. Department of Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem said the body camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide "as funding is available."

At least seven people have been shot dead during federal immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump launched mass deportations after returning to office following campaign promises of an immigration crackdown.

Affordable Care enrollment plummets in Kansas

The number of Kansans enrolled in an insurance plan available from the Affordable Care Act plummeted by 20% this year following the expiration of enhanced tax credits intended to offset premium costs.

New numbers released last month by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services show that enrollment in insurance plans available from the ACA in Kansas had fallen about 36,000 in February 2026 compared to a year earlier.

The data showed that 143,880 Kansans were enrolled in the ACA as of February 2026 compared to 179,920 in February 2025.

Data crunched by healthcare think tank KFF show that it’s the biggest numerical and percentage decrease for Kansas since the program started a decade ago.

KFF reported that the overall ACA marketplace enrollment fell 13% in a year, dropping to 19.2 million in February 2026 from a high of 22.1 million in 2025.

An analysis conducted by The Associated Press found that Ohio and Oklahoma each saw a more than 32% decline in ACA enrollment over the past year.

The AP reported that those states lost larger shares of their covered populations than any other state.

“Following closely behind, and losing more than a fourth of their enrollees, were Arizona, South Carolina, Minnesota, Indiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Louisiana and Missouri,” The AP reported.

The numbers just released at the end of June are different from the people who signed up for coverage by last January.

The new numbers reflect what’s known as “effectuated enrollment,” which describes the number of people who enrolled in coverage and also paid the premiums required for their coverage to take effect.

Last year, Kansas set a record for the number of people who signed up but didn’t necessarily pay the premium for an insurance plan available from the Affordable Care Act.

It was a 16.7% increase from the 171,376 who enrolled in the ACA in 2024 and almost 3.5 times the 57,013 who enrolled the first year the benefit was available in 2014.

But the record number of Kansans who enrolled last year was anticipated to recede with the expiration of the tax credits.

Five of the companies that provided insurance on the exchanges raised rates this year, anywhere from an average increase of 11.74% to an average increase of 33.4%.

According to KFF, expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits was estimated to increase premium payments by 114%, on average, for subsidized enrollees if they choose to stay in the same plan.

As a result, many were expected to drop their ACA coverage or maybe move to a less-expensive plan on the exchanges.

KFF has estimated that the enhanced premium tax credits saved subsidized enrollees an average of $705 a year in 2024, lowing their payment to $888.

Without the enhanced premium tax credits, annual premium payments in 2024 would have averaged $1,593, according to KFF.

“While the Trump administration attributes this drop in enrollment to their attempts to address fraud, this coverage loss happened at the same time millions of people faced steep increases in their premium payments — often in the double or even triple digits — with the expiration of enhanced tax credits,” wrote Cynthia Cox, senior vice president and director of the program on the ACA for KFF.

“While we do not yet know how many people have become uninsured, the ACA Marketplaces are often an option of last resort for people who do not have an affordable offer of coverage through their work and are ineligible for Medicare or Medicaid,” Cox wrote

The Department of Health and Human Services issued a report saying that growth in ACA enrollment was “improper” or “fraudulent” because individuals misstated their income to gain access to free plans.

“Media reports have focused narrowly on plan cancellations, a routine phenomenon that occurs primarily in the beginning of plan years as individuals are often auto-reenrolled into plans they may no longer want or need,” the HHS report said.

“Historically, 90-95 percent of enrollees who select an ACA Exchange plan during Open Enrollment ultimately effectuate coverage by paying their first premium,” the agency said.

“These reports largely ignore the broader landscape, including that an estimated 2.9 million improperly enrolled individuals have been removed due to various program integrity measures. In addition to the about 1.5 million enrollees CMS previously removed from subsidies, we estimate another 1.4 million either ended coverage or were blocked from coverage due to recent policy changes. Various policies and metrics point to these improper and phantom enrollments being pulled out of the system from late 2025 to early 2026.”

Constitutional amendment and immigration

Supporters of a constitutional amendment calling for the election of justices to the Kansas Supreme Court have introduced a new issue into the campaign: immigration.

A new ad hit the airwaves on Friday criticizing the court for “protecting illegal aliens” and warned that the state Supreme Court isn’t accountable to anyone until now. It told voters that on Aug. 4 they “can keep murderers like this off the street by voting yes on the ‘right to vote’ amendment.”

As of Saturday, the ad was targeted for Wichita and Topeka.

It’s not clear what murderers are being referenced in the ad.

The ad from the social welfare group Kansans for Democracy doesn’t go into details but cites a Topeka Capital-Journal story from March 3, 2020. That was the date the U.S. Supreme Court found that federal immigration law doesn’t override the state’s prosecution of identity theft.

Then-Kansas Attorney General Derek Schmidt had appealed a Kansas Supreme Court decision, which overturned three identity theft convictions because federal law preempted state prosecutions for using false or stolen personal information contained in federal immigration forms. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 5-4 to reverse Kansas state Supreme Court.

“From the beginning of our country, criminal law enforcement has been primarily a responsibility of the states, and that remains true today,” Justice Samuel Alito wrote in the majority opinion.

“Our federal system would be turned upside down if we were to hold that federal criminal law pre-empts state law whenever they overlap,” Alito wrote.

“Indeed, in the vast majority of cases where federal and state laws overlap, allowing the states to prosecute is entirely consistent with federal interests.”

Three years earlier, the Kansas Supreme Court overturned the convictions of three men — Ramiro Garcia, Donaldo Morales and Guadalupe Ochoa-Lara — who could not legally work in the United States.

The three restaurant workers were convicted of identity theft and providing false information on state tax forms or private legal documents.

In a 5-2 ruling, the state Supreme Court concluded that federal immigration law prohibited Kansas from enforcing state criminal law because the information had also been submitted on a federal I-9 form used for employment verification.

The social welfare group financing the ad doesn’t have to disclose its donors under federal law. The group has booked or spent about $1.3 million on television and radio ads during the campaign, according to national ad tracker AdImpact.

Overall so far, an estimated $6.2 million has been spent or booked on broadcast ads for and against the amendment, according to AdImpact. The cost of the campaign is likely much more after campaign mailers, consultants and polling are counted.

Opponents of the amendment have spent about $3.8 million on television as they make a case that the amendment is an attempt to get around court decisions upholding the right to an abortion and provide more money for public education.

They say the amendment will put political donors in front of justices who will decide their cases.

Supporters of the amendment have spent or booked about $2.4 million, according to AdImpact.

Those numbers are fluid and can change as the campaign evolves.

Kansans for Democracy was incorporated by Brandon Smith, who was listed in public records with a Hutchinson address.

Smith is believed to be the former policy director for former Gov. Sam Brownback. He is now in private practice in Nashville, Tennessee.

Smith worked previously as chief of staff and assistant solicitor general for Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti, where he led multistate litigation and high-profile constitutional challenges.

He previously worked as executive director of legislative and regulatory affairs for former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin.

He also was deputy director of the Federalist Society and an adjunct professor at American University.

Congressional fundraising

The state’s congressional incumbents will likely move into the general election with healthy campaign nest eggs compared to their Democratic and Republican challengers, new campaign finance reports show.

The state’s four members of Congress – Tracey Mann in the 1st District, Derek Schmidt in the 2nd District, Sharice Davids in the 3rd District and Ron Estes in the 4th District – each have more than $1 million in cash on hand for the quarter ending June 30.

Davids, the state’s lone Democrat in Congress, reported raising $656,845 in the second quarter.

She raised more than any of her Republican Kansas colleagues on Capitol Hill last quarter She had about $1.7 million in cash on hand at the end of the reporting period.

Davids has primary opposition from Sarah Preu, a technology and communications professional from Fairway.

Democratic challenger Colin McRoberts, who teaches at the University of Kansas, raised $64,665 during the quarter and had $22,877 in cash on hand at the end of reporting period.

McRoberts has primary opposition from Lawrence attorney Lauren Reinhold, who reported raising $16,238 and had about $3,784 in the bank when the reporting period closed.
